origin: The Manes were the collective spirits of the Roman dead, honoured as gentle guardian deities of the family rather than feared ghosts, with festivals like the Parentalia set aside each February to bring them offerings of food and wine. Roman tombstones were often inscribed "Dis Manibus," "to the spirits of the dead," a formula so common that archaeologists still find its abbreviation across the ancient world.

definition: The animal life of a particular region, habitat, or geological period.
origin: Fauna takes its name from Faunus, the Roman god of the countryside and wild creatures, and his sister or consort Fauna, a goddess of fertility and animal life honoured by rural households. Eighteenth-century naturalist Carl Linnaeus borrowed her name as the scientific term for a region's animal life, pairing it with "flora," named for the goddess of flowers.

definition: Relating to hell or the underworld; used informally to express extreme annoyance at something.
origin: Infernal comes from Latin infernus, "of the lower regions," describing the underworld ruled by Pluto that lay literally beneath the earth the living walked upon. From that grim, subterranean realm the word came to describe anything hellish or, in looser modern speech, simply infuriating enough to seem sent from below.

definition: A woman regarded as a prophetess or oracle; someone believed to foretell the future.
origin: The Sibyls were prophetic women scattered across the ancient Mediterranean, believed to be mouthpieces for the gods, and the most famous to Rome was the Sibyl of Cumae, said to have sold Rome's sacred Sibylline Books of prophecy to a king after he refused her price too many times. Roman leaders consulted these guarded books for centuries in times of crisis, and "sibyl" became the lasting word for any female prophet.

definition: Relating to a volcano, or, figuratively, marked by sudden and explosive intensity of emotion.
origin: Volcanic comes from Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and metalworking, who was believed to forge weapons for the gods in a smoking underground smithy beneath Mount Etna in Sicily. Romans explained the mountain's rumbling and eruptions as the sound of Vulcan's hammer at work, and his name gave Italian, then English, the word for any fire-spewing mountain.

definition: All the gods of a particular religion collectively, or a group of especially famous or respected people or things.
origin: Pantheon combines Greek pan, "all," with theos, "god," and named both the full assembly of a religion's deities and the actual Pantheon temple built in Rome around 126 AD to honour them all under one great domed roof. That building's soaring dome still stands nearly two thousand years later, and the word broadened from housing all the gods to describing any celebrated group of greats.

definition: Drowsy or sleepy; tending to induce sleep.
origin: Somnolent comes from Latin somnus, "sleep," the name also given to Somnus, the Roman god of sleep who lived in a dark, silent cave where no rooster crowed and no branch stirred, and whose son Morpheus shaped the dreams of sleepers. From that drowsy god's name Latin built somnolentus, and English kept the word for anything heavy-lidded or sleep-inducing.
